questions.question: How do you write a unit test for a Spring @Service using Mockito?
questions.title: Unit Test Spring Service Mockito | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Use @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) to run the test with Mockito, @Mock to create a mock repository, and @InjectMocks to inject that mock into your service. This is a true unit test—no Spring context loads, runs in milliseconds. Only use @SpringBootTest when you need the full application context for integration testing.

sections.title: Unit Testing Spring Services with Mockito
sections.content:
Unit testing a Spring service means testing the service's business logic in isolation—without loading the entire Spring application context. **Mockito** lets you create mock objects for dependencies like repositories or external APIs, and **MockitoExtension** runs JUnit 5 tests with Mockito support.

The key annotations are **@Mock** (creates a mock dependency), **@InjectMocks** (injects mocks into the service under test), and **@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)** (activates Mockito in JUnit 5). This approach is fast—tests run in 10-50 milliseconds because there's no Spring container startup.

Think of it like testing a single gear in a machine: you control what comes in from connected parts (the mocks) and verify what comes out (the result). This is the foundation of test-driven development in Spring Boot—write hundreds of these fast unit tests to cover business logic, then add a handful of slower integration tests to verify the layers work together.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Pure Unit Test|~No Spring context|the ExtendWith MockitoExtension|Mock the deps|InjectMocks the service
blue|The Flow|~Arrange, act, assert|stub the repository|call the service method|assert and verify
emerald|Why No Context|~Speed and focus|milliseconds not seconds|tests logic only|context means integration

sections.title: Complete Unit Test Example
When to Use This Approach
sections.content:
Use this style when the service's own branching, calculations, or error translation are the subject of the test and its collaborators can be represented by controlled interfaces.

For example, stub a repository to return `Optional.empty()` and assert that the service raises `OrderNotFoundException`; stub a gateway decline and verify that no receipt is sent.

Use a Spring context test separately when the behavior depends on proxies, transactions, configuration binding, validation infrastructure, or actual bean wiring.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Loading Spring unnecessarily**: direct construction is enough for plain service logic.
- **Testing only mock calls**: also assert the service's returned value, state, or exception.
- **Verifying implementation noise**: check only calls that represent an observable requirement.
- **Ignoring error paths**: arrange empty results and collaborator failures as well as success.
- **Expecting annotations without lifecycle support**: initialize `@Mock` fields with the Mockito extension or create mocks programmatically.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)**: Activates Mockito in JUnit 5 tests, enabling @Mock and @InjectMocks annotations
- **@Mock**: Creates a mock object for a dependency—all methods return null/0/false unless you stub them with when()
- **@InjectMocks**: Creates the real service instance and injects all @Mock dependencies into it automatically
- **when().thenReturn()**: Stubs a mock method—defines what the mock should return when called with specific arguments
- **verify()**: Asserts that a mock method was called with expected arguments—crucial for testing side effects

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: To write a unit test for a Spring service using Mockito, you start by annotating the test class with at-ExtendWith MockitoExtension dot class. That's the JUnit 5 way to activate Mockito. Then you create mocks for the service's dependencies using at-Mock. For example, if your OrderService depends on an OrderRepository, you'd write at-Mock private OrderRepository orderRepository. Next, you annotate the service itself with at-InjectMocks, which tells Mockito to create a real OrderService instance and inject the mock repository into it. Inside your test method, you use when and thenReturn to define the mock's behavior. Say when orderRepository dot save is called with any Order, return a saved Order with an ID. Then you call your service method and use JUnit assertions to verify the result. The key thing here is this runs without Spring—no application context, no database connection, nothing. It's pure Java object testing. That's why it's so fast. You can run hundreds of these tests in a couple seconds. One mistake I see freshers make is adding at-SpringBootTest to these tests. That loads the entire Spring application, which takes several seconds per test. For unit testing service logic, you don't need Spring at all. Save at-SpringBootTest for end-to-end integration tests where you're testing the whole application flow.

questions.question: What is the difference between @SpringBootTest and slice test annotations?
questions.title: @SpringBootTest vs Slice Tests Spring Boot | Java Fresher
questions.direct_answer: `@SpringBootTest` builds a broad application context from the application's Spring Boot configuration. Its default `webEnvironment` is `MOCK`, so it does not start a live server unless you choose `RANDOM_PORT` or `DEFINED_PORT`. A slice such as `@WebMvcTest` or `@DataJpaTest` limits configuration to one layer. Pick the narrowest context that proves the behavior.

sections.title: Full Context vs Layered Testing Strategy
sections.content:
`@SpringBootTest` asks Spring Boot to find the application's configuration and create a broad test `ApplicationContext`. It is useful when several layers, bean wiring, configuration properties, or application startup must work together.

It is not automatically an end-to-end HTTP test. The default `webEnvironment = MOCK` creates a web application context without starting a real server. Use `RANDOM_PORT` or `DEFINED_PORT` when the test must send requests through a running server.

A **slice test** limits scanning and auto-configuration to a focused concern. `@WebMvcTest` focuses on Spring MVC, `@DataJpaTest` on JPA repositories and entities, and `@JsonTest` on JSON mapping. Application collaborators outside the slice must be imported or replaced. The best choice is the smallest context that contains the behavior being tested.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|SpringBootTest|~Broad Boot context|MOCK web mode by default|RANDOM_PORT for a server|multi-layer checks
blue|Slice Tests|~Focused context|WebMvcTest, DataJpaTest|restricted configuration|one framework concern
emerald|Pick Rule|~Unit for plain logic|slice for one boundary|broad context for integration|live server only when needed

sections.title: Code Example
SpringBootTest vs Slice Tests Comparison
sections.content:
| Test style | What it creates | Good for | Important boundary |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `@WebMvcTest` | MVC-focused context | routing, validation, JSON, controller advice | service collaborators are imported or overridden |
| `@DataJpaTest` | JPA-focused context | mappings, repository queries, persistence rules | database choice still matters |
| `@SpringBootTest` | broad Boot context | wiring and multi-layer integration | default `MOCK` does not start a server |
| `@SpringBootTest(RANDOM_PORT)` | broad context plus live server | HTTP integration through a real port | still does not include external systems automatically |

sections.title: When to Use Each Approach
sections.content:
Use **`@SpringBootTest`** when the real application configuration and several layers must work together. Add `RANDOM_PORT` when the HTTP server boundary is part of the test; the default `MOCK` mode is enough for broad context tests without a port.

Use **`@WebMvcTest`** for routing, binding, validation, JSON, advice, and security at the MVC boundary. Use **`@DataJpaTest`** for mappings and repository queries, and **`@JsonTest`** for focused Jackson behavior.

Use a plain test with Mockito when the subject is Java business logic and no Spring feature needs to run.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Calling the default an end-to-end test**: `@SpringBootTest` uses a mock web environment unless configured otherwise.
- **Assuming a slice has all application beans**: slices intentionally restrict scanning and auto-configuration.
- **Using the broadest context for simple logic**: a direct unit test is clearer when Spring behavior is irrelevant.
- **Mocking the feature under test**: a repository query test needs the repository and database, not a mocked repository.
- **Ignoring context reuse**: inconsistent properties and bean overrides can create different cache keys.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **`@SpringBootTest`**: broad Boot application context
- **Default web mode**: `MOCK`; no live server
- **Live HTTP**: use `RANDOM_PORT` or `DEFINED_PORT`
- **Slice tests**: focused scanning and auto-configuration for one concern
- **Selection rule**: use the narrowest context that proves the behavior

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: `@SpringBootTest` creates a broad Spring Boot application context, so it is useful for checking bean wiring, configuration, and behavior that crosses layers. It does not automatically make the test end to end: its default web environment is `MOCK`, which creates a web context without a live server. I use `RANDOM_PORT` when I need to send HTTP requests through a real server. Slice tests are narrower. `@WebMvcTest` focuses on MVC behavior, while `@DataJpaTest` focuses on entities and repositories. A slice will not discover every service in the application, so needed collaborators must be imported or replaced. I choose the smallest test context that contains the behavior: a plain unit test for service logic, a slice for one framework layer, and a broad context only for integration across those boundaries.

questions.question: How do you test a Spring REST controller using MockMvc?
questions.title: Spring MockMvc Controller Testing | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Use `@WebMvcTest(Controller.class)` with `MockMvc` to test Spring MVC routing, request binding, validation, serialization, controller advice, and configured filters without a live server. Replace a controller collaborator with current `@MockitoBean` (legacy Boot code uses deprecated `@MockBean`). If Spring Security is present, its filter chain is normally part of the slice, so authenticate the request or deliberately configure the test boundary.

sections.title: Testing REST Controllers with MockMvc
sections.content:
`MockMvc` sends a mock servlet request through Spring MVC without opening a network port. With `@WebMvcTest(OrderController.class)`, Spring loads MVC-focused infrastructure such as the selected controller, converters, validation, controller advice, and eligible filters.

Collaborators outside that slice are not automatically loaded. On current Spring, `@MockitoBean OrderService service` can replace the service required by the controller. Older Spring Boot examples use `@MockBean`, which is deprecated since Boot 3.4.

When Spring Security is on the classpath, the configured security filter chain normally participates. Tests should use a test user, JWT support, CSRF token where appropriate, or an explicit test security configuration. Turning filters off changes what the test proves.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|MockMvc|~Test controllers|no real server|the WebMvcTest slice|the fast HTTP layer
blue|The Flow|~Simulate a request|perform get or post|andExpect a status|assert the JSON
emerald|Mock the Service|~the MockBean annotation|controller in isolation|stub service calls|verify the mapping

sections.title: Complete Controller Test Example
When to Use This Approach
sections.content:
Use a `@WebMvcTest` when the question is about MVC behavior: URL mapping, status codes, request validation, JSON conversion, exception handling, or security at the web boundary.

Use a plain unit test when the controller is just a Java method and framework behavior is irrelevant. Use `@SpringBootTest(RANDOM_PORT)` when the real server stack and broader application wiring must participate.

`MockMvcBuilders.standaloneSetup(controller)` is another narrow option, but it only contains the advice, converters, filters, and other MVC pieces that the test explicitly registers.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Calling it a plain unit test**: a `@WebMvcTest` still creates a Spring test context.
- **Forgetting collaborators**: services outside the MVC slice must be imported or overridden.
- **Ignoring security**: a request can return 401 or 403 before reaching the controller.
- **Forgetting CSRF**: state-changing requests with CSRF protection enabled need a valid test token.
- **Overstating standalone setup**: it does not reproduce every MVC component unless configured.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **MockMvc**: exercises the servlet/MVC pipeline without a network port
- **`@WebMvcTest`**: focused MVC test context for selected controllers
- **Collaborators**: override with `@MockitoBean` on current Spring; `@MockBean` is legacy Boot
- **Security**: filters normally participate when Spring Security is configured
- **Boundary**: use a live-server test when the real server stack matters

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: I use `@WebMvcTest(OrderController.class)` with `MockMvc` when I need to test the HTTP-to-controller boundary without starting a server. It can check mappings, query and path binding, bean validation, JSON, controller advice, and configured filters. The service is outside the MVC slice, so on current Spring I replace it with `@MockitoBean OrderService`; older Boot projects use the now-deprecated `@MockBean`. A request such as `mockMvc.perform(get("/orders/7"))` can then assert the status and JSON body. If Spring Security is configured, its filters normally run too, so the test supplies an authenticated user or JWT and a CSRF token for protected state-changing requests. I would not silently disable filters because that changes the boundary being verified. A live-server test is more suitable when the real network/server stack is part of the requirement.

questions.question: How do you test a Spring Data JPA repository?
questions.title: Spring Data JPA Repository Testing | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Use `@DataJpaTest` to test entity mappings, repository queries, and persistence behavior in a JPA-focused Spring context. Tests are transactional and normally roll back, and Boot commonly replaces the configured data source with an available embedded database. That replacement is not guaranteed to behave like production; use the production database through Testcontainers and disable replacement when dialect-specific behavior matters.

sections.title: Testing JPA Repositories with Real Database
sections.content:
`@DataJpaTest` creates a focused context for JPA entities, repositories, and related persistence configuration. It is designed for tests that execute real repository and ORM behavior rather than mocking the repository.

By default, these tests are transactional and normally roll back after each test. Spring Boot also tries to replace the application's data source with an available embedded test database. That is often H2 only because H2 is a common test dependency; the annotation itself does not promise H2.

An embedded substitute can miss SQL dialect, collation, locking, JSON, index, or transaction behavior from production. When those details matter, run the production database type in Testcontainers and use `@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = Replace.NONE)`. Flush and clear the persistence context when the test must prove that SQL is executed and data is read back rather than served from the first-level cache.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|the DataJpaTest slice|~Repository layer only|in-memory or Testcontainers|rolls back per test|fast
blue|What to Test|~Custom queries|derived methods|JPQL correctness|not Spring's plumbing
emerald|Gotcha|~Don't mock the repo|use a real DB slice|test the actual SQL|trust generated CRUD

sections.title: Complete Repository Test Example
When to Use This Approach
sections.content:
Use `@DataJpaTest` for derived queries, custom JPQL or native queries, entity mappings, converters, constraints, and persistence lifecycle behavior.

An embedded database is reasonable for portable, simple JPA behavior. Use the production engine through Testcontainers for native SQL, dialect-specific types, locking, generated values, collation, or migration compatibility.

Rollback protects changes made in the test-managed transaction. Work committed in another thread or independent transaction may not be rolled back with the test.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Assuming H2 is automatic**: Boot needs an embedded database dependency or an explicitly configured data source.
- **Treating database products as interchangeable**: H2 success does not prove PostgreSQL or MySQL behavior.
- **Testing only the persistence cache**: use `flush()` and `clear()` when a real database round trip matters.
- **Expecting every side effect to roll back**: independent transactions and external threads are outside the test transaction.
- **Mocking the repository**: that tests service logic, not JPA mappings or queries.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **`@DataJpaTest`**: focused JPA context with real repository behavior
- **Transactions**: tests normally roll back after completion
- **Database replacement**: Boot uses an available embedded database when configured to replace
- **Production fidelity**: use Testcontainers plus `replace = NONE` when dialect behavior matters
- **Database round trip**: flush and clear when cache could hide an error

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: I use `@DataJpaTest` when I want to test entities, mappings, and repository queries with real JPA behavior. The test is transactional and normally rolls back after each method. Spring Boot commonly replaces the data source with an embedded database if one is available, but the annotation does not guarantee H2. For a simple portable JPQL query, an embedded database may be enough. For PostgreSQL JSON columns, locking, native SQL, collation, or generated-value behavior, I use a PostgreSQL Testcontainer and disable replacement with `@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = NONE)`. I also call `flush()` and clear the persistence context when I need to prove SQL was executed and the row can be read back, not just returned from the first-level cache. A mocked repository would not test any of those JPA contracts.

questions.question: What is the difference between @Mock and @MockBean in Spring Boot tests?
questions.title: @Mock vs @MockBean in Spring Boot
questions.direct_answer: `@Mock` creates a standalone Mockito mock. The older Spring Boot `@MockBean` overrides a bean in a Spring test context; since Boot 3.4 it is deprecated for removal in 4.0 in favor of Spring Framework's `@MockitoBean`. Use `@Mock` with direct constructor wiring for unit tests, and a bean override only when Spring creates the object that needs the mock.

sections.title: Two Ways to Mock in Spring Boot Tests
sections.content:
`@Mock` belongs to Mockito and creates an object outside Spring. A unit test passes it directly to the class under test.

The older Spring Boot `@MockBean` creates or replaces a bean inside a Spring test context. Since Spring Boot 3.4, it is deprecated for removal in Boot 4.0 in favor of Spring Framework's `@MockitoBean`. That replacement is visible to objects constructed and injected by Spring.

The Spring test annotation creates the context; the bean override changes its contents. Different override declarations can lead to different context-cache keys, so tests reuse contexts best when their configuration stays consistent.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|the Mock annotation|~Plain Mockito|no context|fast unit tests|the ExtendWith extension
blue|the MockBean annotation|~Spring context|swaps a real bean|integration or slice|slower
emerald|Pick Rule|~Mock for pure logic|MockBean with SpringBootTest|or slice tests|don't mix carelessly

sections.title: Code Example
@Mock vs @MockBean Comparison
sections.content:
| Point | `@Mock` | `@MockitoBean` / legacy `@MockBean` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Owner | Mockito | Spring TestContext / older Boot |
| Registered in Spring | No | Yes, as a bean override |
| Wiring | direct constructor or Mockito injection | Spring injects it into context-managed objects |
| Typical use | unit test | slice or broader context test |
| Current status | current | `@MockitoBean` current; `@MockBean` deprecated in Boot 3.4 |

sections.title: When to Use Each Annotation
sections.content:
Use **`@Mock`** when a test constructs the subject directly and Spring behavior is not part of the requirement.

Use **`@MockitoBean`**—or legacy `@MockBean` on an older Boot baseline—when a slice or broad Spring test needs a context-managed object to receive a mock replacement.

Do not choose by assumed speed numbers. Choose based on whether the framework context is part of the behavior being proved.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using a bean override without a Spring test context**
- **Expecting a plain `@Mock` to be autowired into Spring beans**
- **Loading Spring when direct constructor wiring is enough**
- **Using deprecated `@MockBean` in new code on a current Spring baseline**
- **Claiming the override always destroys the cache**: override declarations instead contribute to context configuration and reuse

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **`@Mock`**: Mockito-only object outside Spring
- **`@MockitoBean`**: current Spring bean-override annotation
- **`@MockBean`**: older Boot annotation, deprecated since 3.4
- **Plain unit test**: use direct construction and `@Mock`
- **Spring test**: override a bean only when context-managed wiring is required

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: `@Mock` is a Mockito annotation. It creates a standalone mock, and I pass that object directly into the service I am testing. A Spring bean override is needed only when Spring creates the subject. Older Boot code uses `@MockBean`, but since Boot 3.4 that annotation is deprecated for removal in 4.0; current Spring code uses `@MockitoBean`. For example, a plain `OrderServiceTest` can use `@Mock PaymentGateway` and `new OrderService(gateway)`. A `@WebMvcTest` can use `@MockitoBean OrderService` because Spring creates the controller. The context is loaded by the Spring test configuration, not by a plain Mockito annotation. Also, different override configurations can reduce context-cache reuse; it is more accurate than saying every override simply invalidates the cache.

questions.question: How do you test a Spring @Service that has a @Transactional method?
questions.title: Testing a @Transactional Spring Service
questions.direct_answer: For unit tests, mock the repository and test business logic without transactions—@Transactional has no effect without a Spring context. For integration tests, use @DataJpaTest or @SpringBootTest to load the transaction infrastructure, then verify transaction behavior like rollback on exceptions or cascade operations.

sections.title: Testing Transactional Services at Two Levels
sections.content:
Testing a **@Transactional** service requires understanding that the annotation is not Java language behavior—it's a **Spring AOP proxy** that wraps your method in transaction management code. This means there are two distinct testing approaches. **Unit tests** focus on the business logic inside the method: mock the repository, stub its methods, and verify your service's logic works correctly—the @Transactional annotation is ignored because no Spring context exists to create the proxy. **Integration tests** focus on the transactional behavior itself: use @DataJpaTest or @SpringBootTest to load Spring's transaction infrastructure, then verify that transactions commit when methods succeed, roll back when exceptions are thrown, or propagate across multiple repository calls. The common mistake is trying to verify rollback behavior in a unit test—without Spring's transaction proxy active, @Transactional is just a decoration with no runtime effect.

Think of it this way: unit tests verify "what the method does", integration tests verify "how Spring wraps the method in transaction boundaries".

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Unit Test Reality|~No real transaction|Transactional is a proxy|inactive without context|tests logic only
blue|What to Verify|~Behaviour, not rollback|stub the repo|assert the results|verify the save calls
emerald|Rollback Testing|~Needs a context|SpringBootTest|a real or H2 database|integration territory

sections.title: Unit Test Example for Transactional Service
When to Use Each Testing Approach
sections.content: **Use unit tests** (with mocked repositories) when you want to verify the service's business logic, decision-making, and interactions with dependencies—checking that it calls the right repository methods in the right order, handles validation correctly, or throws the right exceptions. These tests are fast and focus on the code you wrote, not Spring's infrastructure. **Use integration tests** (with @DataJpaTest or @SpringBootTest) when you need to verify transactional behavior that only exists at runtime—confirming that multiple repository saves happen in a single transaction, that a RuntimeException triggers a rollback so no data is saved to the database, or that cascade deletes work correctly across entity relationships. Integration tests are slower but catch issues where your transaction boundaries are misconfigured or where lazy-loading triggers unexpected database queries.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Testing transactions without Spring**: a plain Mockito test cannot exercise Spring's transactional proxy.
- **Assuming every exception rolls back**: by default, Spring rolls back for unchecked exceptions; checked-exception behavior needs explicit configuration.
- **Ignoring self-invocation**: a call from one method to another on the same object can bypass proxy interception.
- **Confusing test rollback with service rollback**: a test-managed transaction can hide what would commit in production.
- **Using a broad context for plain validation**: keep business-rule unit tests separate from transaction integration tests.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **@Transactional is a Spring proxy**: The annotation only works when Spring's AOP infrastructure is active, not in plain unit tests
- **Unit test focus**: Mock repositories and test business logic, decision flow, and method interactions—@Transactional is ignored
- **Integration test focus**: Load Spring context with @DataJpaTest or @SpringBootTest to verify transaction commit, rollback, and propagation
- **Rollback verification**: Use integration tests to confirm that exceptions trigger rollback and no data persists to the database
- **Test pyramid principle**: Write more unit tests for business logic (fast, isolated) and fewer integration tests for transaction behavior (slower, comprehensive)

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Testing a Transactional service depends on what you want to verify. For unit tests, you ignore the at-Transactional annotation completely. You mock the repository using at-Mock, stub its methods with Mockito, and test your business logic—like does the service validate the order correctly, does it call save in the right sequence. The at-Transactional annotation doesn't do anything in this context because there's no Spring context to create the transaction proxy. It's just a decoration on the method. For integration tests, you actually need Spring to be running. You'd use at-DataJpaTest if you're testing repository interactions, or at-SpringBootTest if you need the full application context. This loads Spring's transaction infrastructure, so now at-Transactional actually works. You can verify things like: if the method throws an exception, does the transaction roll back so no data is saved to the database. Or if you save multiple entities, do they all commit together in one transaction. The key thing freshers miss is that at-Transactional is a Spring AOP proxy feature—it wraps your method at runtime with transaction management code. Without Spring running, that proxy doesn't exist, so the annotation has no effect. So my approach is: unit tests for business logic with mocks, integration tests for transaction behavior with a real database.

questions.question: How do you test a Spring @Service method that calls an external REST API?
questions.title: Testing Services with External REST Calls
questions.direct_answer: Put an HTTP client behind a small application interface. Unit-test the service by mocking that interface, not by reproducing a fluent `WebClient` chain. Separately test HTTP details—URL, headers, JSON, timeout, and status mapping—against a local stub server such as WireMock or MockWebServer. No real third-party call is needed.

sections.title: Isolating External REST API Calls in Tests
sections.content:
External HTTP code has two useful test boundaries.

For **service logic**, depend on a small interface such as `PricingGateway`. A Mockito mock can return a price or throw a domain exception. The test stays focused on what the service does with that result.

For the **HTTP adapter**, use a local stub server such as WireMock or OkHttp MockWebServer. Point the real `RestClient`, `WebClient`, or `RestTemplate` adapter at that server and assert request paths, headers, payloads, response decoding, timeout handling, and status-to-exception mapping.

Mocking each link in a fluent `WebClient` chain couples the test to call order and generic types. It can pass even when the real request is wrong.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Mock the Client|~No real network|stub RestTemplate or WebClient|deterministic responses|fast tests
blue|Test Scenarios|~Cover all paths|a success response|an error status|a timeout or exception
emerald|Verify|~The right call made|the correct URL and args|an argument captor|retry behaviour

sections.title: Mocking RestTemplate in Service Test
When to Use Each Testing Approach
sections.content:
Use Mockito for business decisions around the external result: retry policy delegation, fallback choice, price calculation, or domain error mapping.

Use a local HTTP stub server for the adapter contract: URL construction, authentication headers, JSON conversion, 4xx/5xx handling, delayed responses, and malformed bodies.

Keep a small number of broader tests for configuration and wiring. Do not call a real vendor from ordinary automated tests unless the test environment and vendor explicitly support that contract.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Mocking a fluent chain**: tests become tied to `WebClient` implementation details.
- **Testing only the happy response**: cover timeout, connection failure, 4xx, 5xx, and invalid JSON where relevant.
- **Calling the real service**: tests become slow, rate-limited, costly, and nondeterministic.
- **Asserting only a return value**: adapter tests should also verify the outgoing HTTP contract.
- **Retrying everything**: retries must follow idempotency and error policy; do not hide this in the mock setup.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Service unit test**: mock a small gateway interface
- **Adapter test**: run the real HTTP client against a local stub server
- **Verify**: URL, headers, body, decoding, status mapping, and timeouts
- **Avoid**: deep mocks of fluent client chains
- **No real vendor dependency**: ordinary tests stay local and deterministic

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: I separate the business service from the HTTP adapter. The service depends on a small interface such as `PricingGateway`, so its unit test can mock one method and check what the service does with a price or error. Then I test the real HTTP adapter against a local WireMock or MockWebServer instance. That second test proves the URL, headers, JSON body, response mapping, timeout, and 4xx or 5xx behavior without contacting the vendor. I avoid mocking every `WebClient` step because that verifies an implementation chain rather than the actual HTTP request. For failures, I include the cases the production policy handles—such as timeout, malformed JSON, and a retryable server response—and I keep retry behavior consistent with whether the request is safe to repeat.

questions.question: How do you test exception handling in a Spring @Service — for example, when a repository throws a DataAccessException?
questions.title: Testing Exception Handling in Spring Services
questions.direct_answer: Stub the mock to throw the exception using when().thenThrow(), then use assertThrows() from JUnit 5 to verify that your service throws the expected exception or handles it correctly. Test both propagation—service re-throws the exception—and translation—service wraps the exception in a domain-specific exception.

sections.title: Testing the Unhappy Path with Exceptions
sections.content:
Exception handling is where many production bugs hide—code that only runs when dependencies fail. To test it, you **stub your mocked dependency to throw an exception** using Mockito's **when().thenThrow()**, then verify your service responds correctly.

There are two common patterns: **propagation** where your service re-throws the exception unchanged (letting it bubble up to the controller or caller), and **translation** where your service catches the exception and wraps it in a **custom domain exception** with additional context. For example, when the repository throws **DataAccessException**, your service might catch it and throw **OrderNotFoundException** with the order ID and a user-friendly message. You verify this with **assertThrows()** from JUnit 5, which captures the thrown exception so you can assert on its type, message, and cause. Testing exceptions ensures your error handling code is correct and gives you confidence that your service fails gracefully when the database is down or returns unexpected errors.

sections.title: At a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Stub the Failure|~Force an error|then throw on the mock|simulate a downstream fail|trigger the catch
blue|Assert the Outcome|~assertThrows|check the exception type|verify the message|wrapped or rethrown
emerald|Verify Side Effects|~What happens on error|no commit|the error is logged|a fallback is called

sections.title: Testing Exception Handling in Service
When to Test Each Exception Pattern
sections.content: **Test propagation** when your service is a thin wrapper around a repository and you want infrastructure exceptions to bubble up unchanged—like a simple CRUD service where DataAccessException is meaningful to the caller and will be handled by a global exception handler in the controller layer. Verify that the service doesn't accidentally swallow or change the exception. **Test translation** when your service adds business logic and the low-level exception isn't meaningful to callers—like catching EmptyResultDataAccessException and throwing OrderNotFoundException with the specific order ID that failed. This gives better error messages and hides infrastructure details from the API layer. You should test both the exception type and the message content, and verify that the original exception is preserved as the cause for debugging.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Only testing the happy path**: Freshers write tests where everything succeeds—repository returns data, external API responds—but never test what happens when dependencies throw exceptions, leaving error handling code with zero test coverage.
- **Using try-catch in tests**: Developers write try-catch blocks in test methods to capture exceptions, making tests verbose and easy to get wrong—JUnit 5's assertThrows is cleaner and returns the exception for further assertions.
- **Not verifying the exception message or cause**: Tests assert that the right exception type is thrown but don't check the message or wrapped cause, missing bugs where error context is lost or the wrong exception is wrapped.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **when().thenThrow()**: Stub mocked dependencies to throw exceptions simulating failure scenarios like database errors or timeouts
- **assertThrows()**: JUnit 5 method that verifies an exception is thrown and returns it for additional assertions on message or cause
- **Propagation pattern**: Service re-throws the exception unchanged—test that the original exception escapes unmodified
- **Translation pattern**: Service catches low-level exception and throws a domain-specific exception with context—test message and cause
- **Test negative paths**: Exception handling is where bugs hide—always test error cases, not just success scenarios

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: To test exception handling in a service, you stub the mock dependency to throw an exception using when-thenThrow. For example, if you're testing a service that calls a repository, you'd mock the repository and make findById throw a DataAccessException to simulate a database failure. Then you use assertThrows from JUnit 5 to verify your service handles it correctly. assertThrows takes the expected exception class and a lambda that calls your service method. If that exception is thrown, the test passes and assertThrows returns the exception so you can make additional assertions on it. There are two patterns you typically test. The first is propagation, where your service just lets the exception bubble up unchanged. You'd verify that the same exception type escapes the service. The second is translation, where your service catches the low-level exception and wraps it in a custom domain exception with more context. For example, catching DataAccessException and throwing OrderNotFoundException with the specific order ID that failed. In that case, you'd assert on the custom exception type, check that the message includes the order ID, and verify that the original exception is preserved as the cause using getCause. The common mistake freshers make is only testing the happy path—when everything works—and leaving all the catch blocks untested. That tanks your code coverage and means your error handling code has never actually run until it fails in production.
